messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 43

Martha is a 78-year-old woman who has been a graphic designer for over fifty years. She still works part-time from the home she shares with her husband of fifty-three years, Arthur, in a quiet coastal town. She came to see me at the urging of her daughter, who noticed that Martha had stopped going to the beach—something she had done every morning for decades.

The trauma happened three years ago, in late autumn. A storm surge, unprecedented in the town’s recorded history, swept through the low-lying neighborhoods just before dawn. Martha remembers the sound first: a deep, groaning roar that was not the wind but the earth itself shifting under water. She and Arthur had only minutes to gather their dog and climb to the attic. From the small window, she watched their garden shed lift off the ground and float away like a toy. The water rose to the second step of the attic stairs before it stopped.

They were rescued by a neighbor in a small boat six hours later. The house was still standing, but the first floor was gutted. Martha’s design studio—a converted sunroom where she had worked for thirty years—was destroyed. Her drafting table, her Pantone swatches, her carefully organized flat files of client work, all of it was soaked, swollen, and coated in silt.

In the months that followed, Martha threw herself into the rebuilding. She was practical, efficient, and grateful. She told friends she was lucky. She told herself the same thing. But she began to notice small changes.

She cannot look at the weather forecast anymore. If she hears the word “storm” on the radio, her chest tightens and her hands go cold. She stopped checking the tide tables, which she used to do every week to plan her beach walks. Now, if she accidentally sees a photograph of the ocean, she feels a jolt of fear, as if the image itself might spill water into the room.

Her work has become difficult in ways she cannot explain. She used to love designing logos with organic, flowing lines—curves that suggested waves or wind. Now, she finds herself avoiding those shapes. She catches herself drawing hard angles, sharp corners, straight lines. She tells clients she is moving toward a “more modern aesthetic,” but she knows the truth. Curves feel dangerous. They feel like the shape of water rising.

She has nightmares, though she does not call them that. She tells me she has “bad dreams” about the attic. In the dreams, the water keeps rising. It reaches the third step, then the fourth. In the most recent one, it touched her feet before she woke up gasping, her heart pounding so hard she thought she was having a heart attack. Arthur has learned not to touch her when she wakes like that. She flinches.

She avoids the sunroom. It has been rebuilt, but she moved her desk into a corner of the living room. She tells Arthur the light is better there. She knows it is not true. The sunroom has too many windows. She cannot sit in a room with that much glass without scanning the horizon for a wall of water that will never come.

Yesterday, her daughter asked her to design a poster for a local charity event. The theme is “Resilience.” Martha agreed, but she has not started. She has been staring at a blank screen for three days. She tells herself she is just blocked, that every designer has dry spells. But she knows the real problem. She does not know how to draw resilience without drawing the water that taught it to her. And she is not ready to draw that water. She is not sure she ever will be.

She is still Martha. She still makes Arthur laugh. She still takes her dog for short walks, though she avoids the path that leads to the beach. She is functional, pleasant, and deeply tired. She came to therapy because her daughter asked, but also because she is tired of being afraid of the weather. She is tired of flinching when Arthur turns on the faucet. She is tired of designing a life made of straight lines.
